title: Human factors and multidisciplinary teamwork
blurb: Explain why skilled midwives still make errors, match each error type to the fix that works, and use team training and shared awareness to keep women and babies safe.
question: Twice in a month a midwife on the labour ward has picked up ergometrine instead of oxytocin from boxes stored side by side; both were caught at the check. What is the most effective response?

teach.body: The Code (19.2) uses the Health and Safety Executive definition: human factors are environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work in a way that can affect health and safety. SPM 5.4 asks midwives to apply human factors, environmental factors and strength-based approaches when working with colleagues. In plain English: errors come from the work as well as the worker, so redesign the work rather than just telling people to try harder.

teach.h: Error types and the fix that works
head: Type
What happens
Best fix
rows: Find out why the rule is bypassed
teach.caption: HSE human failure types. Reminders to 'be careful' fix none of them well.
HSE: job, individual and organisation all shape behaviour at work.

teach.body: Ockenden's immediate and essential action on multidisciplinary training says staff who work together must train together. East Kent's Reading the signals named teamworking with a common purpose as one of its four areas for action. SPM 5.8 asks midwives to understand why interdisciplinary team working and learning matters. Multidisciplinary skills drills, such as PROMPT obstetric emergency training, rehearse roles, equipment and communication before a real emergency.
teach.cite: Ockenden final report (2022), action 7; Reading the signals (2022); SPM 5.8

teach.body: Situational awareness is knowing what is happening around you and what may happen next; shared situational awareness is a common understanding across the team. Communication failure is a common finding in NHS serious incident investigations. In an unpredictable situation (SPM 5.13.6), name the emergency out loud, call for help early, say who is leading, and give the team a short summary of what is happening and the plan.
teach.cite: SPM 5.13.6; NHS England, Improving safety critical spoken communication

teach.body: Midwife Priya finds that ergometrine and oxytocin ampoules sit in near-identical boxes side by side, and twice this month the wrong one was picked up and caught at the check. These are slips: the plan was right, the action went wrong. Priya reports both near misses, moves the boxes apart, adds shelf labels and asks pharmacy whether supply can change. A memo telling midwives to 'be more careful' would not remove the trap.

rows.label: Ask what went well in a smooth emergency, and why
Use each team member's skills and experience
Give specific, positive feedback alongside improvements

teach.note: SPM 5.3 includes sharing learning from positive as well as adverse outcomes.

teach.text: Slip versus mistake: a slip is the right plan carried out wrongly (fix the design); a mistake is the wrong plan (fix knowledge and procedures). And a violation is usually a workaround for a broken system, so ask why before you blame.

items: Human factors: job, individual and organisational factors that shape behaviour at work (HSE; Code 19.2).
Slips and lapses are fixed by design; mistakes by training; violations by finding out why rules are bypassed.
Ockenden: staff who work together must train together; East Kent: teamworking with a common purpose.
In an emergency: name it, call for help early, make the leader clear and share the plan aloud.
Strength-based approaches learn from what goes well as well as what goes wrong.

summary: You can now classify errors using human factors thinking and pick the fix that actually works. You can also explain why maternity teams train together and how shared situational awareness keeps a team safe in an unpredictable emergency.

A.q: Which statement best matches the definition of human factors used in the NMC Code?
options: Personal qualities that make a good midwife
Mistakes caused by not following policy
How women respond to the care they get
Work and personal factors that shape safety
A.why: Code 19.2 uses the HSE definition: environmental, organisational and job factors, and human and individual characteristics, which influence behaviour at work and can affect safety.

whyNot.0: Human factors are not a list of personal virtues; they include the work system.
whyNot.1: Not following policy is one kind of failure, not the definition.
whyNot.2: Human factors concern staff behaviour at work, not women's reactions.

A.q: A midwife who knows the correct dose draws up the wrong ampoule from two look-alike boxes stored together. What type of error is this?
options: A slip
A mistake
A violation
A lapse
A.why: A slip is an unintended action in a familiar task: the plan was right, the action went wrong. Fix it through design.

whyNot.1: A mistake is a wrong plan, often a knowledge gap; she knew the correct dose.
whyNot.2: A violation is a deliberate deviation; this was unintended.
whyNot.3: A lapse is a forgotten step, not picking the wrong item.

A.q: According to the Ockenden report, how should multidisciplinary maternity staff train for obstetric emergencies?
options: Each profession trains in its own group
Midwives complete online modules each year
Senior staff attend and cascade to others
Staff who work together train together
A.why: Ockenden action 7: staff who work together must train together.

whyNot.0: Separate professional training is what Ockenden wanted to move away from.
whyNot.1: Online modules alone do not rehearse teamwork.
whyNot.2: Cascading does not give the whole team shared practice.

B.q: An audit finds midwives often skip the hourly fresh eyes CTG review at night. What should the labour ward lead do first?
options: Issue written warnings to the midwives
Remove fresh eyes from the night policy
Find out why the review is being missed
Ask the midwives to sign the policy again
B.why: Deviations from a rule are usually workarounds for a system problem, such as no second midwife being free. Understand the cause before deciding the fix.

whyNot.0: Warnings do not remove the cause and discourage honest reporting.
whyNot.1: Fresh eyes at least hourly is part of Saving Babies' Lives v3; removing it reduces safety.
whyNot.3: Re-signing does not address why the review is missed.

B.q: During a postpartum haemorrhage, several staff arrive in the room at once. Which action best builds shared situational awareness?
options: Each person checks the notes for themselves
The most senior doctor takes over silently
The midwife writes a full record before speaking
The leader states the problem and plan aloud
B.why: Shared situational awareness is a common understanding across the team: a clear leader summarising the situation and plan aloud creates it.

whyNot.0: Separate note checks waste time and give no common picture.
whyNot.1: Taking over without a summary leaves the team without a shared understanding.
whyNot.2: Records are completed as soon as possible, but the team needs the information now.

B.q: A shoulder dystocia drill on the labour ward went smoothly and the baby was born quickly. How does a strength-based approach use this event?
options: It needs no review as the outcome was good
The team agrees it was lucky and moves on
The team identifies what went well and why
The shift leader reviews the records
B.why: SPM 5.4 asks for strength-based approaches and SPM 5.3 for sharing learning from positive outcomes: understanding what worked lets the team repeat it.

whyNot.0: Good outcomes still hold learning about what made them good.
whyNot.1: Calling it luck loses the learning about what worked.
whyNot.3: Learning from success involves the whole team, not one person reading notes.

C.q: A newly qualified midwife sets up an oxytocin infusion using a regimen from her previous trust, which differs from local guidance. The error is caught. What type of error is this and what is the best fix?
options: A slip; separate the infusion bags
A violation; start a disciplinary process
A lapse; add a reminder to the checklist
A mistake; training on the local guideline
C.why: She followed the wrong plan in good faith: a mistake, which is reduced through training and clear procedures.

whyNot.0: A slip is a right plan done wrongly; here the plan itself was wrong.
whyNot.1: A violation is deliberate; she did not knowingly deviate.
whyNot.2: A lapse is a forgotten step; nothing was forgotten.

C.q: A midwife at a home birth recognises shoulder dystocia. A second midwife is present. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Ask the partner to time the head-to-body interval
Name the emergency aloud and call for help
Apply fundal pressure to deliver the shoulders
Try gentle traction for one more contraction
C.why: In an unpredictable situation, name it and call for help early so the team and ambulance are mobilised; then McRoberts and suprapubic pressure (RCOG GTG42).

whyNot.0: Timing matters, but calling for help comes first.
whyNot.2: Fundal pressure must not be used in shoulder dystocia.
whyNot.3: Only axial traction is used, and repeated pulling delays help.

C.q: A midwife preparing intravenous antibiotics on the postnatal ward is interrupted three times and forgets to add the diluent. Which change will most reduce this risk?
options: Protect medicine preparation from interruptions
Ask her to complete a reflective account
Display a poster about concentration
Move her to a different ward
C.why: Forgetting a step after interruption is a lapse; lapses are reduced by design, such as protecting medicine preparation from interruptions.

whyNot.1: Reflection may help her learning but does not remove the cause.
whyNot.2: Posters ask people to try harder rather than changing the work.
whyNot.3: Moving her leaves the system problem in place for others.

reteach.title: Fix the trap, not the person
reteach.question: If a good midwife falls into the same trap twice, what needs to change?

blocks.h: The trap stays until you move it
blocks.body: Skilled people still slip when boxes look alike, when they are interrupted, or when they are tired. Human factors thinking asks what in the job, the person and the organisation made the error likely, and changes that. Training fixes wrong plans; design fixes slips and lapses; understanding the cause fixes workarounds.

blocks.text: 'Remind staff to be more careful' is the classic wrong answer to a human factors question.

explain.body: The HSE groups human factors into the job (task, workload, environment), the individual (skills, fatigue, stress) and the organisation (staffing, culture, leadership).

test.q: Which of these is an organisational human factor?
options: A midwife's tiredness after a night shift
Two drugs in similar packaging
A culture where staff fear reporting
A midwife's years of experience
test.why: Culture, staffing and leadership are organisational factors.

whyNot.1: Packaging is a job or task factor.

explain.body: Both are unintended actions in familiar tasks. A slip is doing the wrong thing (wrong ampoule); a lapse is forgetting a step (missed diluent). Both are reduced by design.

test.q: A midwife forgets to restart a woman's CTG after helping her to the toilet. Which error type is this?
options: A violation
A lapse
A mistake
A slip
test.why: Forgetting a step in a familiar task is a lapse.

whyNot.0: A violation is a deliberate deviation.
whyNot.2: A mistake is a wrong plan; her plan was right.
whyNot.3: A slip is doing the wrong action, not forgetting one.

explain.body: Reading the signals (East Kent, 2022) named four areas for action, including teamworking with a common purpose. Multidisciplinary drills build that shared purpose.

items.label: fix what got in the way

test.q: Which of these is one of the four areas for action in the East Kent report Reading the signals?
options: Expanding midwife-led units
Teamworking with a common purpose
Reducing caesarean birth rates
Introducing continuity of carer
test.why: The four areas are identifying poorly performing units, giving care with compassion and kindness, teamworking with a common purpose, and responding to challenge with honesty.

whyNot.0: Midwife-led units are not one of the four areas.
whyNot.2: Caesarean rates are not one of the four areas.
whyNot.3: Continuity of carer is not one of the four areas.

explain.body: NHS England notes that communication failure is a common finding in serious incident investigations. Clear, structured, spoken information protects women and babies.

test.q: What does NHS England report about communication in serious incident investigations?
options: It is a rare contributory factor
It matters mainly in community care
It is a common finding
It is mostly about written records
test.why: NHS England: communication failure is a common finding in serious incident investigations.

whyNot.1: It is found across settings, not mainly in the community.
whyNot.3: NHS England's work concerns spoken communication.
